narrative:
An attacker at 192.168.92.129 ran a short, three-step recon session against 192.168.92.131 between 08:39 and 08:42 UTC. First, a top-1000-port nmap scan with service/version detection and default scripts (-sV -sC) found SSH open and, because of -sC, automatically ran NSE scripts like ssh2-enum-algos/ssh-hostkey against it. Second, a full 1-65535 port scan with the same flags took nearly two minutes and triggered a second, nearly identical probe of the SSH service near its end. Third, the attacker looked up local exploit-db entries for "OpenSSH 9.3" with searchsploit - a purely offline, local action.

On the target, only an ssh.log was available (clock offset ~2 hours from the attacker's UTC). It showed two bursts of exactly 8 connections each from 192.168.92.129, seconds apart, at 10:39:48-50 and again at 10:41:43-45. Every connection died before authentication: some closed immediately, two tried SSHv1 and were rejected, and four each offered a different host-key algorithm (ssh-dss, ssh-rsa, ecdsa-sha2-nistp384, ecdsa-sha2-nistp521) and were refused for "no matching host key type." These two bursts line up with the two nmap scans' SSH-script executions. No usernames, passwords, or successful logins ever appeared - this was pure protocol/algorithm fingerprinting, not brute-forcing.

The searchsploit lookup, by contrast, left no trace anywhere in target logs, since it never touched the network - it's a local database query on the attacker's own box.

The lesson: network scans against open services generate loud, correlatable pre-auth noise even without credentials ever being tried, while local attacker-side reconnaissance (exploit-db lookups) is invisible to the target and would require attacker-side telemetry to observe.

steps.note: Nmap's default -sV/-sC against top-1000 ports ran at 08:39:43-08:39:53 UTC from the attacker clock. The target's sshd log (in a timezone offset by ~2 hours from the attacker's UTC clock, giving 10:39:48-10:39:50) shows an 8-connection burst against port 22 within the same ~2 second window, consisting of banner-exchange failures, protocol-version mismatches (SSHv1 probe), and host-key algorithm enumeration (ssh-dss, ssh-rsa, ecdsa-sha2-nistp384, ecdsa-sha2-nistp521) - this is exactly the signature of nmap's ssh2-enum-algos/ssh-hostkey NSE scripts invoked by -sC/-sV against the open SSH port discovered in the top-1000 port scan.
steps.detection: Enable sshd verbose/debug logging and alert on bursts of multiple connections from one source IP within a few seconds that never complete key exchange (fail2ban or a SIEM correlation rule on repeated 'Unable to negotiate'/'banner exchange' lines); also deploy a network IDS (Suricata/Zeek) signature for nmap NSE ssh-enum-algos traffic pattern, and monitor firewall/NetFlow for a single source touching 1000 ports in under 10 seconds (classic SYN/connect scan fingerprint).

steps.note: The full port-range scan (-p 1-65535, 08:39:58-08:41:49 UTC attacker time) took almost 2 minutes and, because -sC/-sV were again specified, re-ran the same NSE SSH scripts once port 22 was confirmed open a second time near the end of the scan. This produced a second identical 8-connection burst at 10:41:43-10:41:45 target time, matching the tail end of the full-port scan's duration and reproducing the exact same algorithm-offer sequence (ssh-dss, ssh-rsa, ecdsa-sha2-nistp384, ecdsa-sha2-nistp521) seen in step 1.
steps.detection: Same as step 1: connection-rate alerting per source IP on sshd, plus network-level detection of a full 65535-port scan (very high distinct-port-count from one source in a short window) via NetFlow/IDS - this is a much louder, higher-confidence indicator than the top-1000 scan and should trigger immediate alerting (e.g., Suricata 'ET SCAN' signatures or a SIEM rule for >1000 distinct destination ports from one source in under 5 minutes).

steps.note: searchsploit is a local, offline lookup against a static exploit-database copy on the attacker's own machine; it makes no network connection to the target, so it is structurally impossible for this to appear in any target-side log, including ssh.log.
steps.detection: Not detectable from target-side logs. The only way to observe this step would be endpoint monitoring/EDR or shell-history auditing on the attacker's own machine, which is out of scope for the target's log sources; alternatively, infer intent from subsequent exploitation attempts against the specific OpenSSH 9.3 CVEs it would have surfaced.

detection_ideas.idea: Alert on bursts of multiple SSH connections from a single source IP that terminate before authentication (pre-auth closes, banner-exchange failures, kex negotiation failures) within a short time window - this is the clearest signature of SSH fingerprinting/enumeration tools (nmap NSE, ssh-audit) and precedes real brute-force or exploit attempts.
detection_ideas.data_source: sshd auth/verbose log (syslog/journald) correlated via SIEM

detection_ideas.idea: Deploy fail2ban or equivalent with a short ban threshold tuned to catch rapid pre-auth connection churn, not just failed logins, since this scan never reached the authentication stage.

Add network-level scan detection (NetFlow/Zeek/Suricata) to flag a single source IP contacting many distinct ports (top-1000 or full 65535) on one host within seconds to minutes - this would have caught step 1 and step 2 even before the SSH log entries existed.

Expand log collection beyond ssh.log: enable firewall/connection logging and web/application logs on the target so that the full scope of a recon campaign (not just SSH) can be correlated for a given source IP.
detection_ideas.data_source: host firewall logs, additional service logs
